name: ChessMas
oneLiner: Two LLM agents play chess, and move legality is decided solely by a deterministic rules engine.
summary: A port of the `llm-multi-agent-chess` prototype from Python and Streamlit to .NET 10, assembled by {{term:aspire|Aspire}} 13.4.6 out of six source projects and two test projects. Each side of the board is an independent `AIAgent` from {{term:maf|Microsoft Agent Framework}} 1.15.0, and the choice of backend (Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Foundry, local Ollama or a human) is an entry in `appsettings`, not a branch in the code. The most important decision fits in one sentence: `ChessMas.Engine` is the only authority on legality. The agent calls `get_board_state`, gets a FEN together with the full list of legal moves in UCI and SAN, proposes a move through `propose_move`, and `TryApplyMove` matches the proposal against a `Move` object generated by the engine instead of parsing a string. That is a direct answer to the failure mode of the original prototype, in which the model reconstructed the position from prose and lost track of the board. Cost accounting against real `AgentRunResponse.Usage` and four {{term:otel|OTel}} metrics are bolted on, but the whole thing has **four commits, no persistence and no recorded evidence that a game was ever played here with a real model**.
tests: 26 `[Fact]` methods and zero `[Theory]` across two projects: 15 for the engine, 5 for the cost arithmetic, 6 for the human move gate. None of them needs an API key; the number that pass has not been verified, because what was counted is attributes, not runs.
ci: `ci.yml` does a restore, a Release build and `dotnet test` with the trx logger and an upload of the results artefact; no Docker and no secrets. `pages.yml` publishes the `docs/` directory to GitHub Pages, and `dependabot.yml` watches NuGet weekly in three groups. The CHANGELOG records that the workflow initially triggered on `main` while the default branch was `master`, so for a while it never ran at all.

metrics.label: Model backends selectable in the UI

docs.label: Changelog listing the guessed APIs that did not exist

components.name: HumanMoveGate
components.description: The bridge between a loop running in the background and a synchronous HTTP request: one `TaskCompletionSource` per turn, re-armed after every rejection, with a registry keyed by `gameId` and side. The orchestrator suspends on an `await` instead of polling, and the 91 lines know nothing about chess.

components.name: ChessMas.ServiceDefaults
components.description: {{term:servicedefaults|The shared Aspire project}}: export of traces and metrics over OTLP, health checks, service discovery and `HttpClient` resilience. No domain entities, copyable into any .NET solution.

components.name: GameCostTracker + ModelPricingCatalog
components.description: Multiplies real `AgentRunResponse.Usage` by the price list in the `ModelPricing` configuration section. A model with no entry reports `null`, never USD 0, and every price entry carries a dated `Note` field with its source. It is not portable without rework: `GameCostTracker.cs` has `using ChessMas.Engine;`, and the domain type `ChessMas.Engine.Side` sits in the public surface — `RecordPly(int plyNumber, Side side, long inputTokens, long outputTokens)`, the record `PlyCost(int PlyNumber, Side Side, long InputTokens, long OutputTokens, decimal? EstimatedCostUsd)` and, through the `ByPly` list, `GameCostSummary` as well. `ModelPricingCatalog` on its own is free of it.

components.name: ChessMas.Engine
components.description: The {{term:determinizm|deterministic}} authority on the rules. `GetSnapshot` returns a FEN, the list of legal moves in UCI and SAN, a check flag and the history; `TryApplyMove` is the only place where the board state changes. SAN is computed on a helper board reconstructed from the FEN, so as not to touch the live position.

components.name: ChessMas.Agents
components.description: The tool boundary. `ChessTools` exposes `GetBoardState` and `ProposeMove` as `AIFunction`, each instance bound to one side, so the white agent has no physical way to propose a move for black. The factory has two construction paths: through {{term:ichatclient|IChatClient}} and through `AIProjectClient.AsAIAgent` for Foundry.

components.name: GameOrchestrator + minimal API
components.description: An explicit `while` loop rather than a MAF Workflow graph, because the end condition is judged by the engine, not the model. Five endpoints (`POST /games`, `GET .../state`, `/outcome`, `/cost`, `POST .../move`) and 276 lines without a single test.

components.name: ChessMetrics
components.description: Three counters and a histogram: `chess.moves.proposed`, `chess.moves.rejected`, `chess.ply.duration_ms`, `chess.games.completed`, tagged by side and status. The rejected-proposal rate is intended here as raw material for ranking backends.

components.name: ChessMas.Web
components.description: Blazor Server with a board drawn from scratch out of the FEN field, without any external JS library, and clickable chips of the legal moves for the human. It polls the orchestrator every 400 ms during its own turn and every 1 s otherwise.

overlaps.reason: A direct port of that Python/Streamlit prototype; the README names it as the source and describes which failure mode of that version this architecture fixes.
The README and a comment in `ChessMetrics` point to CopilotScope as the source of the pattern: Aspire composition, OTel from day one, and the approach to scoring.
Both measure model behaviour in an agent loop and count token cost, except that ChessMas does it on a single task and says itself that it is not a benchmark.
The same subject, Microsoft Agent Framework in .NET, from the side of working code rather than book text: `AsAIAgent` and `AIFunctionFactory` are used here and described there.

product: No buyer, and the README closes that route itself, saying that this is not a benchmark of playing strength, that one game proves nothing, and that the cost is an estimate against a price list, not an invoice. This is a credibility project: it shows that the author assembles an agent system in .NET with a hard deterministic boundary, telemetry and cost accounting. If anything here has market value it is `HumanMoveGate` as a human-in-the-loop pattern that knows nothing about chess, and `GameCostTracker` with its configurable price list — but the second only once the `Side` enum has been cut out of its signatures.
highlights: `TryApplyMove` matches the proposal against `Move` objects generated by the engine rather than parsing a string. A human move and an agent move go down **exactly the same path**, with no separate 'trust the human' branch.

The CHANGELOG documents that the project originally did not compile at all, because it was written without the SDK and NuGet, and it names the guessed `ChessDotNetCore` APIs that did not exist: the namespace, `CurrentPlayer`, `MoveType`, `Promotion` as `char?`. Rare honesty in a public repo.
A library trap, written down: castling is emitted twice, as `e1g1` and as the chess960 `e1h1`. Only the standard form reaches the list shown to the model; both are accepted on input.
Underpromotion is modelled as four separate moves (`a7a8q/r/b/n`) rather than a flag, which is a direct consequence of discovering that `Move.Promotion` is a `char?`.

A model with no entry in the price list reports `null` rather than USD 0.00, the UI shows that difference, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` enforces it as invariant no. 4. The whole `ChessDotNetCore` surface is confined to one file, and that is a written-down invariant too.
gaps: **No evidence that a game was ever played here with a real model.** There is no transcript, no screenshot and no saved result, so the entire agent layer is empirically unchecked.
`GameOrchestrator` runs to 276 lines and is the most complex file in the repo, and there is not one test on it. The 26 tests cover the engine, the costs and the human gate.
No persistence and no eviction: games, results and cost trackers live in a `ConcurrentDictionary` that is never cleared. `SECURITY.md` calls this unbounded growth itself.
No authentication on the orchestrator API and no limit on concurrent games. The limits of 200 plies and 5 rejections protect one game; nothing protects the bill.
`POST /games` starts the loop through `Task.Run` without observing exceptions, so a failure of the game loop has nowhere to surface.

The GitHub Pages site cannot be confirmed from the repository, so it has been taken off the links: `pages.yml` says in its own comment that without a one-off Settings -> Pages -> Source: "GitHub Actions" setting the workflow runs and only then fails to deploy. There is no `gh-pages` branch in the repo and no record of a successful deployment, and the existence of the workflow alone is evidence of intent, not of a published site. The site's source sits in `docs/index.html` and can be viewed there.
next: Write `GameOrchestrator` tests with a fake `AIAgent` substituted in. The loop, the rejection limit, the forfeit and the human path are deterministic and need no model; this is the largest hole in coverage.
Play one full agent-versus-agent game and record it in the repo, with a transcript, a rejection count and a cost. Without that the whole thing is an unrun sketch.
Add a TTL or a cap on the number of games in memory, and minimal authentication on the orchestrator, even a shared token, before anything stands outside localhost.
Replace `Task.Run` with a `BackgroundService` or a queue that logs the exception and sets the game status to `failed`.

Cut `GameCostTracker` and `ModelPricingCatalog` out into a separate project with no provider dependencies; a comment in the test csproj suggests this itself, and it is the only candidate for a package in this repo.
risks: `Microsoft.Agents.AI.Foundry 1.15.0-preview.260722.1` and `Azure.AI.Projects 2.1.0-beta.4` are pins on prerelease. The README describes NuGet's downgrade block as the reason it is not possible to drop back to the stable 2.0.1, and announces breaking changes itself.
No authentication plus no spending limit means an exposed instance is an open card on the owner's API account. `SECURITY.md` says so outright, but that is still the default state of the code.

`ChessDotNetCore 1.6.0` is a small single-maintainer library whose surface changed between versions. Confining it to one file limits the cost of migration, not the risk of the upstream being abandoned.

Four commits and the last one from 31 July 2026: without further activity the repository will read as a one-off burst, and the prices in `appsettings.json` age on their own, with one entry marked outright as unverified.
headline: The hard-boundary architecture is done, but nobody has played a single game here
